entries.definition: A joint NASA and ISRO Earth observation mission that carries L-band and S-band imaging radars.
entries.example: The Curuai layers in this app come from the mission’s L-band radar.

entries.definition: An imaging radar that sends microwave pulses toward Earth and combines many echoes as the satellite moves to make a detailed picture. It can work at night and through most clouds.
entries.example: The grayscale NISAR image shows the strength of the radar return across the study area.

entries.definition: A radar image that stores both how strong the echo was and where it was in its wave cycle. Keeping both lets scientists compare the waves later.
entries.example: Use the SLC product family in catalogue discovery when an analysis needs phase. The prepared GCOV backgrounds show signal power.

entries.definition: A radar image still arranged by distance and direction from the satellite. It keeps the strength and timing within each wave.
entries.example: The product filter can find RSLC records when you need complex radar-coordinate data.

entries.definition: A radar image placed on a map grid that keeps both echo strength and the position in each wave cycle.
entries.example: A live GSLC catalogue result represents a different product type from the measured GCOV backscatter rows in the date matrix.

entries.definition: A NISAR product that puts radar measurements on a map. It includes echo strength for channels such as HH and HV, with adjustments for terrain.
entries.example: The app reads the HHHH or HVHV power layer to make an HH or HV map and its dB measurements.

entries.definition: A NISAR product that uses the patterns in two radar passes to estimate how the surface moved along the satellite’s viewing direction.
entries.example: Use the product filter to identify GUNW records separately from the single-date GCOV images in the matrix.

entries.definition: A mapped estimate of how far a visible radar pattern shifted between two observations. It can help track larger movements.
entries.example: A GOFF discovery result describes a paired displacement product. The Radar change chart compares GCOV return strength in dB.

entries.definition: A NISAR product that estimates the amount of water in the upper part of the soil using the radar return and other information.
entries.example: Choose SME2 in catalogue discovery to look for estimated soil moisture. Choose GCOV for measured radar backscatter layers and their charts.

aliases: Alaska Satellite Facility Distributed Active Archive Center
entries.definition: A NASA data archive operated by the University of Alaska Fairbanks that distributes NISAR radar products and maintains their documentation.
entries.example: Open an ASF product link in Source audit to trace a row to its catalogue record.

entries.definition: The provider’s product readiness designation. NISAR uses BETA for early data, PROVISIONAL for calibrated and partially validated data, and VALIDATED for fully calibrated and validated products.
entries.example: A date can have a prepared layer that passed this app’s local checks while belonging to a PROVISIONAL provider collection. Source audit describes the provider release.

entries.definition: An adjustment that makes radar brightness easier to compare between slopes. A slope facing the satellite can look brighter partly because of its shape.
entries.example: GCOV applies RTC before the app summarizes HH or HV backscatter. Extreme terrain geometry can still leave masked pixels.

entries.definition: Radar echo strength expressed in a standard way so images can be compared more fairly. Use the same channel and processing when you compare.
entries.example: The app’s GCOV layers share key NRB characteristics, including geocoding, calibrated backscatter and supporting quality information.

entries.definition: The orientation in which the radar wave vibrates. Radar can send a wave in one orientation and listen for an echo in the same or a different orientation.
entries.example: The matrix separates HH, HV, VH and VV because each channel measures a different transmit and receive combination.

entries.definition: The radar sends the horizontal part of the wave and listens for the horizontal part of the echo. Both letters stand for horizontal.
entries.example: Select HH to show the horizontal co-polarized Curuai observations and their saved measurements.

entries.definition: The radar sends a horizontally oriented wave and listens for the vertical part of the echo. Plants and rough surfaces can scatter part of the echo into that second orientation.
entries.example: Select HV to inspect cross-polarized return on a Curuai date where that channel is available.

entries.definition: The radar sends a vertically oriented wave and listens for the horizontal part of the echo.
entries.example: A VH column without an image for a selected acquisition means the app lacks a prepared VH layer for that observation.

entries.definition: The radar sends a vertically oriented wave and listens for the vertical part of the echo.
entries.example: Use the VV column to check availability for a particular date before comparing images or numbers.

entries.definition: A polarization channel in which the radar transmits and receives the same orientation. HH and VV are the two linear co-polarized channels.
entries.example: The Qeshm chart uses HH, a co-polarized measurement of the radar return.

entries.definition: A polarization channel in which the radar transmits one orientation and receives the perpendicular component. Vegetation and other complex surfaces can redirect part of the signal into this component.
entries.example: Curuai HV is a cross-polarized layer. Compare HV with HV across dates to keep the measurement type consistent.

entries.definition: An acquisition mode that records two polarization channels. In a standard linear mode these can be HH and HV or VV and VH.
entries.example: An HH/HV date can populate two matrix columns. Availability of VV and VH is tracked separately.

entries.definition: A radar mode that records all four linear transmit and receive combinations, HH, HV, VH and VV.
entries.example: A four-column matrix lets you check which channels are available on each date. The acquisition mode tells you which combinations the radar collected.

entries.definition: The longer-wavelength radar band used by NISAR’s L-SAR instrument, with waves about 24 cm long.
entries.example: The Qeshm and Curuai local measurements are from NISAR L-band acquisitions.

entries.definition: The shorter-wavelength radar band used by NISAR’s S-SAR instrument, with waves about 9.4 cm long.
entries.example: Check the Wavelength field before treating a discovered S-band record as comparable to a prepared L-band series.

entries.definition: The primary frequency group within a NISAR instrument’s product. Its bandwidth, available channels and grid size depend on the acquisition mode.
entries.example: The measured Curuai HH crop uses L-band Frequency A.

entries.definition: A separate frequency group that may be present within the same instrument band, often with narrower bandwidth and a coarser product grid. NISAR primarily collects Frequency B for atmospheric corrections.
entries.example: A record containing L-band Frequency B still refers to L-SAR. Check the group before comparing its grid or channels with Frequency A.

entries.definition: The width of the frequency interval covered by the transmitted signal. A wider signal bandwidth can resolve finer differences in radar range when the viewing geometry and processing allow.
entries.example: Qeshm Frequency A uses a 20 MHz signal. The MHz value is bandwidth, while the grid spacing is measured in metres.

entries.definition: The distance between successive peaks of a wave. A radar’s wavelength helps determine how it interacts with features of different sizes and materials.
entries.example: The Wavelength and Frequency fields describe different properties. L-band Frequency A is one group of measurements made with the roughly 24 cm L-band radar.

entries.definition: An interval during which the satellite collects the radar data used to create a product. Its timestamp refers to sensing time.
entries.example: Curuai’s August 13 and October 12 rows refer to when NISAR observed the area in 2026.

entries.definition: The date and time when the satellite collected the image, written using Coordinated Universal Time so people in different time zones can compare it.
entries.example: The timestamp 2026-08-13T09:21:54Z marks a Curuai acquisition at 09:21:54 UTC.

entries.definition: A number for a recurring orbital path in NISAR’s observation plan. It helps identify acquisitions that follow similar paths over the same area.
entries.example: The Marañón February 24 and March 8 observations both use track 147.

entries.definition: A numbered scene segment along a track used to organize products. The track and frame together identify a recurring nominal scene location.
entries.example: The two Marañón rows share track 147 and frame 175. The change measurement also checks their aligned grids and shared usable pixels.

entries.definition: One traversal of the satellite over a region, following part of its orbital path. A pass can collect radar data over many neighbouring scene frames.
entries.example: Dates on the same track can represent different passes. Check both the sensing date and the ascending or descending direction.

entries.definition: The satellite observes while travelling generally northward along its orbit.
entries.example: The three Qeshm observations are ascending. Use that field with track, frame and radar mode when checking comparability.

entries.definition: The satellite observes while travelling generally southward along its orbit.
entries.example: The July 12 Burgas observation is descending. Its geometry differs from a typical ascending view of the same region.

entries.definition: The side of the flight path toward which the radar points. The look side and direction of travel together determine which slopes face the beam.
entries.example: NISAR looks left of the flight path. Source audit pairs the look side with the orbit direction when that metadata is available.

entries.definition: Observations made with comparable orbital path, scene framing and viewing direction. Pixelwise comparisons also require aligned grids and compatible measurement settings.
entries.example: The Qeshm time series uses one established track and frame and a common crop. Source audit records the available metadata and comparison limits.

entries.definition: The angle between the incoming radar beam and a line perpendicular to the reference surface. A local incidence angle uses the slope at that location.
entries.example: Even the same surface can return a different signal from a different angle. The app checks geometry before paired change analysis.

entries.definition: In a radar image, the direction along the flight path. The radar builds fine azimuth detail from pulses gathered during flight.
entries.example: RSLC stores data in radar coordinates. The app’s prepared GCOV map is already geocoded.

entries.definition: The straight-line distance from the radar to the target, estimated from the pulse travel time.
entries.example: GCOV maps observations onto ground coordinates so that a location in the map can be matched to an acquisition crop.

entries.definition: Distance across the ground in the direction away from the flight path. It is related to slant range through viewing geometry.
entries.example: The map display uses ground locations. Sensor-coordinate products can use slant-range distance in their stored arrays.

entries.definition: The strip of Earth’s surface observed by the radar along the satellite’s flight path.
entries.example: A catalogue record can cover a long stretch of a swath while the app serves a small study crop from it.

entries.definition: The interval after which a satellite returns to a similar orbital path. NISAR’s planned orbit repeat is 12 days. Usable observations depend on the observation schedule and data availability.
entries.example: Read the actual acquisition dates in the chart. The Qeshm dates include a 24-day gap and a 12-day gap.

entries.definition: An area hidden from the side-looking radar beam by terrain. The radar has no direct view of the shadowed ground.
entries.example: A dark or masked patch near steep terrain can reflect imaging geometry. Check flags before assigning an environmental cause.

entries.definition: A distortion on a steep radar-facing slope where high terrain is closer to the radar than lower terrain and echoes from multiple ground positions overlap.
entries.example: In paired measurements, the app can exclude cells marked by the product’s layover and shadow flags.

entries.definition: The compression of a radar-facing slope in the radar image because different points on it have similar distances to the sensor.
entries.example: Bright or compact terrain features can arise from viewing geometry. Compare calibrated scenes with compatible geometry before interpreting change.

entries.definition: The part of the radar signal that bounces back to the satellite. Roughness, moisture, plants, and the viewing angle can all affect how much comes back.
entries.example: Backscatter over time summarizes the calibrated return of a selected polarization across the study grid.

inline.meaning: the radar echo that returns to the satellite

entries.definition: A way to express radar echo strength that accounts for the area facing the sensor. The NISAR map product also adjusts for terrain.
entries.example: The app can report a gamma nought value as linear power in a scientific GeoTIFF or as dB in a chart.

inline.meaning: radar echo strength adjusted for how much area faces the sensor

entries.definition: A way to express how much radar echo comes back for a given area on the ground.
entries.example: Check the calibration convention before comparing numbers from another sensor with the app’s GCOV gamma nought values.

entries.definition: A ratio-scale representation of radar power. Doubling the value doubles the represented return power under the same calibration. Positive values can be converted to dB.
entries.example: A linear gamma nought value of 0.01 corresponds to −20 dB. The chart and the scientific raster can therefore express the same measurement on different scales.

entries.definition: A scale for comparing how strong two signals are. When comparing radar power, about 3 dB more means twice the power.
entries.example: A value of −20 dB corresponds to 0.01 times the reference power. An increase of about 3 dB corresponds to roughly twice the power.

inline.meaning: a scale for comparing echo strength

entries.definition: Processing that converts instrument readings into a defined measure of radar return power. Use the calibration convention when comparing products.
entries.example: The app reads stored calibrated GCOV values for measurements. Map brightness is produced by applying a display scale.

entries.definition: The grainy pattern in a radar image caused by many tiny echoes adding together or cancelling each other.
entries.example: The chart summarizes many pixels because individual bright or dark cells can fluctuate due to speckle.

inline.meaning: the grainy pattern made by many small echoes

entries.definition: An indication of how many radar samples contribute to a processed cell. Combining looks typically reduces speckle and can trade spatial detail for a more stable estimate.
entries.example: When available, the GCOV looks layer helps document which parts of a prepared crop provide usable measurements.

entries.definition: The middle reading when you put the values in order from smallest to largest. With two readings in the middle, take their average.
entries.example: The Curuai HH chart shows median backscatter near −18.53 dB on August 13, 2026, across the shared valid cells.

entries.definition: The 10th percentile is a value at or below which roughly one-tenth of the measurements lie. It describes the lower part of the distribution.
entries.example: P10 is the lower edge of the chart’s P10–P90 band. That edge shows spread across pixels.

entries.definition: The 90th percentile is a value at or below which roughly nine-tenths of the measurements lie. It describes the upper part of the distribution.
entries.example: The chart band from P10 to P90 spans the middle roughly 80% of measured pixel values. It describes spatial variability.

entries.definition: A difference in calibrated backscatter between two acquisitions. In a paired map, each cell uses the later dB value minus the earlier dB value at the same position.
entries.example: Positive change means a stronger radar return. The Radar change legend shows where change crosses the selected threshold.

entries.definition: Matching spots on the ground that have a usable radar value on every date being compared.
entries.example: The Curuai HH comparison uses 562,500 shared usable pixels. The count is the denominator for cell-level change percentages.

entries.definition: A display and summary threshold for change in power. A +3 dB change is roughly twice the power and a −3 dB change is roughly half the power.
entries.example: Orange denotes stronger cells at or above +3 dB and olive denotes weaker cells at or below −3 dB in the Radar change overlay.

entries.definition: Measurements shown in the order they were taken. In this app, each dot is a date the satellite actually observed. Time between dots can have no recorded values.
entries.example: The Qeshm HH series contains three measured dates on the same crop. Connecting line segments link those dates without providing intermediate satellite measurements.

entries.definition: A conversion from a chosen range of scientific values to visible shades. The same value can look brighter or darker under a different stretch.
entries.example: Check the displayed dB range before comparing grayscale images. Use the GeoTIFF or the chart for calibrated numbers.

entries.definition: How strong the measured echo is compared with the instrument’s background noise. A low ratio means the two are hard to separate.
entries.example: The oil-screening methods check whether the signal is safely above the available noise estimate before interpreting low-backscatter features.

inline.meaning: echo strength compared with instrument noise

entries.definition: A measure of how faint an echo can be before it gets hard to tell apart from the radar’s own noise.
entries.example: The Source audit records when a Harmony subset lacks a spatial noise layer. A value gated against noise needs a noise estimate in a compatible calibration convention.

inline.meaning: the level where faint echoes compete with instrument noise

entries.definition: An area where water at or near the surface regularly shapes the soil, vegetation and habitat. Wetlands can look dry during part of the year.
entries.example: A marsh at Shark River Slough may remain wetland habitat when an optical image shows little visible water.

entries.definition: A wetland dominated by rooted plants whose stems or leaves rise above shallow water or wet soil.
entries.example: Sawgrass can rise above water in the Everglades and obscure it in an optical view.

entries.definition: Water whose surface is visible to an optical sensor through clear air and without vegetation covering it.
entries.example: The Curuai optical comparison tests visible lake water. Water beneath a thick plant canopy can remain unresolved.

entries.definition: Water covering the land or ground surface. It can occur routinely in a wetland or during a flood.
entries.example: Water can inundate the ground beneath marsh plants even if a satellite photo mainly shows green leaves.

entries.definition: The area covered by floodwater at a specific time or water level. Establishing it requires distinguishing floodwater from water already present.
entries.example: An ordinary lake outline shows water extent. Comparing it with a flood-date reference can help isolate newly flooded area.

entries.definition: Low land alongside a river or stream that can be inundated when its water level rises.
entries.example: The Curuai floodplain can gain or lose water during the Amazon's seasonal rise and fall.

entries.definition: Water retreat that commonly happens during the falling-water phase of a seasonal cycle.
entries.example: A smaller lake on an October image can be part of the usual seasonal pattern. Compare Octobers and gauge records before attributing the cause.

entries.definition: A sustained shortage of water relative to what is usual for a place and season. Hydrological drought is often assessed with streamflow, lakes, reservoirs or groundwater.
entries.example: An August–October decrease in lake area needs seasonal or historical context before it can support a drought interpretation.

entries.definition: The timing, duration and recurrence of flooding or water saturation at a site.
entries.example: A year of daily Everglades depth maps can help estimate how long a marsh cell stays inundated.

entries.definition: An instrument or station that measures water level at a particular location.
entries.example: The Óbidos gauge helps describe the regional Amazon water level. Curuai's local lake level needs its own evidence.

entries.definition: The height of the water surface above a reference zero at a gauge. That zero can be different from the riverbed or sea level.
entries.example: A 141 cm reading at one gauge is 141 cm above its own zero. It gives the actual depth only if that zero coincides with the bed.

entries.definition: The vertical distance from the water surface to the ground or bed. A model can estimate it by subtracting ground elevation from water-surface elevation.
entries.example: A 10 cm EDEN class threshold separates modeled values for a marsh comparison at 400 m.

entries.definition: A USGS network of gauges and models that provides gridded daily water levels and estimated depths across the freshwater Everglades.
entries.example: A modeled 400 m EDEN depth cell can serve as an independent comparison for a radar prediction over emergent marsh.

entries.definition: A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service map inventory that classifies wetlands and deepwater habitats.
entries.example: The Everglades benchmark uses NWI to select mapped emergent marsh, then uses EDEN for the comparison date's water estimate.

entries.definition: A wetland designated as internationally important under the Convention on Wetlands.
entries.example: The Atanasovsko Lake Ramsar boundary describes the designated site. Wet and dry surfaces within it vary by date.

entries.definition: A release of petroleum or petroleum products into the environment. The spill's presence, source or extent can require field evidence or corroborating observations.
entries.example: A radar image can reveal dark water worth reviewing after a reported tanker release.

entries.definition: A layer of oil spread across water. It can damp small ripples and cause weaker radar returns under suitable wind and viewing conditions.
entries.example: An elongated dark patch may be a slick candidate. Local wind and an independent observation can help interpret it.

entries.definition: A feature that resembles a floating oil slick in imagery even though it can come from another cause, such as calm wind, natural films or rain effects.
entries.example: A sheltered bay can appear dark along its coast because weak winds leave the water smooth.

entries.definition: The depth of an oil layer on the water surface. Estimating it requires observations and methods that can distinguish thickness and related effects.
entries.example: An ordinary dark patch in the backscatter layer does not tell you how thick a suspected slick is.

entries.definition: A mapped boundary from a report, inspection or independent image. Its meaning and coverage depend on the source and time.
entries.example: A NOAA analyst outline shows an interpreted feature at its reference time. NISAR may have passed before or after it.

entries.definition: A NOAA analyst report describing a possible marine pollution anomaly observed in satellite imagery.
entries.example: An MPSR can supply an independent outline and image time for comparing a NISAR dark-water flag.

entries.definition: An optical index calculated as green minus shortwave infrared reflectance, divided by their sum. It can help distinguish visible water from many surrounding surfaces.
entries.example: The Curuai comparison requires agreement between MNDWI and optical scene classification before using a cell as reference water.

entries.definition: A Sentinel-2 Level-2A map assigning classes such as water, vegetation, cloud, shadow and snow to optical observations.
entries.example: Cloud and shadow classes help remove unreliable cells from the independent Curuai water reference.

entries.definition: The reference elevation a measuring station uses as zero for reported stage. It is specific to the station unless readings are converted to a shared vertical reference.
entries.example: Two stations can report the same gage height while their water surfaces are at different elevations.

entries.definition: A related measurement used when the thing you want to know is difficult to measure directly.
entries.example: A clear optical water label is a proxy for exposed surface water. It can miss water under vegetation and may be measured hours after radar.

entries.definition: Evidence from a source separate from the radar model or its prediction. The comparison is strongest when both sources cover the same target, place and time.
entries.example: The Curuai HH/HV screen uses only NISAR inputs. A separate Sentinel-2 optical scene supplies the water labels for comparison.

entries.definition: Directly observed reference information about the target, ideally aligned to the place and time being tested. Its sampling and measurement limits still matter.
entries.example: A field measurement of water depth at a dated location is direct evidence there. Daily modeled depths between stations remain estimates.

entries.definition: A reference that identifies some positives while leaving the classes of other areas unknown.
entries.example: A published oil outline supports counting flags inside it. Water outside the outline may be clean, unreviewed or affected.

entries.definition: A location or object flagged by a rule as worth inspecting because its measured properties fit some criteria.
entries.example: A dark-water candidate may match a local contrast rule, while calm water or a natural film can explain the same flag.

entries.definition: When a model leaves a place unclassified because the evidence is too weak or missing.
entries.example: Atanasovsko's measured HH and HV remain viewable, but the wetland screen withholds its decision when the local radar noise floor exceeds the eligibility limit.

inline.meaning: no prediction where evidence is too weak

entries.definition: The pixels or cells that satisfy a particular analysis's requirements. Totals depend on quality rules, available reference labels and grid overlap.
entries.example: If cloud removes 200 optical labels and radar quality excludes another 100 independent cells, only the remaining cells count in the comparison.

entries.definition: A measured value or derived quantity used as an input by the model.
entries.example: Curuai's two-feature model uses HH power in dB and the difference between HH and HV in dB.

entries.definition: A class assigned to a training or test item according to an evidence source and labeling rule.
entries.example: A clear optical cell with a water scene class and a compatible MNDWI value can receive the exposed-water label.

entries.definition: Choosing model parameters using example inputs and their targets or a stated fitting rule.
entries.example: The August Curuai labels and NISAR power features were used to learn two logistic coefficients and an intercept.

entries.definition: Checking how a model performs on data separated from fitting. Some validation data help pick settings, while the final test should be kept apart from those choices.
entries.example: The app reports August testing on buffered spatial blocks excluded from fitting and October testing on a separate acquisition date.

entries.definition: Observations reserved for checking performance after model fitting. A final holdout is kept separate from choices about thresholds and features.
entries.example: A test on Curuai's October acquisition uses the August model with its settings unchanged.

entries.definition: A test that keeps whole geographic regions out of training to reduce similarity between nearby training and test examples.
entries.example: The Curuai test withholds alternating three-kilometre blocks and excludes boundary neighbours from the split.

entries.definition: A test using acquisitions from dates or periods outside the model's training period.
entries.example: Fitting Curuai in August and scoring the October scene checks transfer to a new date at the same location.

entries.definition: Evaluating a completed model with independently sourced examples from outside its original study, such as a new geographic site and date.
entries.example: Applying the frozen Curuai model in Bulgaria tests a new setting. Atanasovsko's radar noise restriction leaves that particular test unassessable.

entries.definition: Information from the final test influences model fitting or the choices made before reporting its score, which can overstate performance.
entries.example: Tuning the HH cutoff after seeing October's score would make that October result an unsuitable final holdout.

entries.definition: A model whose features, learned settings and decision rules stay fixed for evaluation.
entries.example: The October assessment uses the August −15 dB HH threshold without changing it after seeing the October optical labels.

entries.definition: A value used to turn a measurement or model score into a class according to a rule.
entries.example: The Curuai HH baseline flags eligible cells at or below −15 dB as exposed water.

entries.definition: A classification method that learns how to combine input features and turn the combined value into a score for a class.
entries.example: The Curuai logistic classifier combines HH and HH minus HV to score exposed water. The published screen uses a fixed score cutoff.

entries.definition: A reference method used to judge whether a newer or more complex model improves performance on the same task and test data.
entries.example: The simple frozen HH rule provides a baseline for the HH/HV and local-texture models at Curuai.

entries.definition: Checking or adjusting model probabilities so they match observed frequencies on comparable examples.
entries.example: If 100 comparable cells receive a calibrated 70% water probability, roughly 70 should be water on average. A raw decision score has no such guarantee.

entries.definition: A stated level of support or certainty for a result. It can come from an analyst's assessment, a calibrated probability, or another defined scoring rule.
entries.example: NOAA analyst confidence and a radar decision score describe different kinds of evidence. Read the stated scale before interpreting either.

entries.definition: A cell the model flags as the target and the comparison reference also labels as that target.
entries.example: The Curuai orange agreement outline marks cells flagged as water by radar and labelled exposed water by the optical reference.

entries.definition: A model flag where a usable reference labels the same cell as outside the target class.
entries.example: A radar water flag in a clear cell labelled other by the optical proxy counts as a false positive for that comparison.

entries.definition: A reference-positive cell the model classifies outside the target. The cell must be valid for assessment.
entries.example: If the clear optical reference labels an eligible cell as water and the radar screen assigns other, that is a missed water cell.

entries.definition: A cell where both the model and a usable reference assign a class outside the target.
entries.example: An eligible cell classified as other by both radar and the optical water reference is a true negative for the water class.

entries.definition: A table comparing model classes with reference classes. For one target class it counts agreeing water, missed water, extra flags and agreed other surfaces.
entries.example: The four counts let you see whether low water overlap is mostly caused by extra flags or by missed reference water.

entries.definition: The fraction of assessed model-positive cells also labelled positive by the reference. It is true positives divided by true positives plus false positives.
entries.example: If 20 cells are flagged and 12 agree with the reference, precision is 60% for those assessed flags.

entries.definition: The fraction of reference-positive cells found by the model. It is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives.
entries.example: If the reference labels 15 eligible cells as water and radar flags 12, recall is 80%.

entries.definition: The fraction of assessed reference-negative cells correctly classified as outside the target.
entries.example: If 90 out of 100 optically clear other-surface cells avoid a radar water flag, specificity is 90%.

entries.definition: The area where the model and reference both found the target, divided by the area where either found it. A bigger share means more agreement.
entries.example: Eight agreeing water cells, two missed and ten extra flags give an IoU of 8 out of 20, or 40%.

inline.meaning: the share of flagged area where both sources agree

entries.definition: The fraction of assessed reference-negative cells that the model flags as positive.
entries.example: Eleven flags among 100 optically labelled other-surface cells give an 11% false-positive rate.

entries.definition: The location and extent chosen for a search or an analysis.
entries.example: A study box around Atanasovsko can contain the lake, land and nearby ponds. It defines the question's map area.

entries.definition: A rectangle given by its outer coordinate limits. In the app's geographic search, the order is west, south, east, north.
entries.example: A broad box can retrieve a scene even if some parts of the rectangle contain no usable radar pixels.

entries.definition: A polygon describing the extent of a satellite scene or another spatial dataset. It may include locations that fail the analysis quality rules.
entries.example: An ASF search can return a footprint over your site. The data file and its masks show which pixels are actually usable.

entries.definition: The portion of a specified area or set of cells for which a condition is true, such as having usable radar data or enough evidence to score a model.
entries.example: A scene can cover the entire map crop while cloud leaves only part of it assessable against an optical reference.

entries.definition: A dataset drawn as a distinct part of the map, with its own geometry, rendering and visibility.
entries.example: The measured radar image, independent optical outline and background coastline can be displayed as separate layers.

entries.definition: A map layer drawn over other layers to show an additional dataset or result.
entries.example: The October Curuai outline is an overlay showing locations where the radar screen and optical water proxy agree.

entries.definition: The map's explanation of its colours, line styles and symbols, including any values or classes they represent.
entries.example: A dashed line for an independent optical reference and a solid water-agreement line have different meanings even if both are orange.

entries.definition: The background map that helps orient you with geographical features such as coasts, rivers and place names.
entries.example: In the viewer the coastline stays visible beneath the dated NISAR radar layer. Its shape comes from a separate map dataset.

entries.definition: A grid of pixels or cells. Each position stores a value or class, and georeferencing places it on Earth.
entries.example: The Curuai HH GeoTIFF is a raster whose cells store radar power.

entries.definition: Geographic data represented as points, lines or polygons with associated information.
entries.example: The outline of a confirmed study area can be stored as a polygon, and a gauge as a point.

entries.definition: Relating image positions to real-world coordinates so the data can line up with other geographic layers.
entries.example: A radar grid records its coordinate system and where its rows and columns fall on the map.

entries.definition: The rules that give coordinates a meaning on Earth, including the reference surface, coordinate axes and any map projection.
entries.example: The Curuai analysis uses a local projected CRS with metres. The browser draws the scene on its own map grid.

entries.definition: An identifier from the EPSG registry that specifies a coordinate reference system or another geodetic definition.
entries.example: EPSG:32721 specifies WGS 84 / UTM zone 21S, the metre-based grid used to calculate Curuai agreement areas.

entries.definition: A mathematical rule for mapping positions on Earth's curved surface to flat coordinates. Projections differ in how they distort shape, area or distance.
entries.example: The browser uses Web Mercator for display, while the original radar and area analysis use an appropriate UTM grid.

entries.definition: Parameters describing how pixel rows and columns map to real-world coordinates. They specify a starting corner, cell spacing and any rotation.
entries.example: A north-up 60 m Curuai grid steps 60 m east for each column and 60 m south for each row.

entries.definition: The coordinate system and pixel layout of the source product before a local reprojecting, resampling or aggregation step.
entries.example: The original Curuai radar values are on a 20 m NISAR grid. The model groups those values into 60 m assessment cells.

entries.definition: The distance between neighboring pixel centers. It describes the grid spacing and can differ from the sensor's effective spatial resolution.
entries.example: Three adjacent 20 m postings span a 60 m analysis cell, while the ability to resolve a small target also depends on the sensor and processing.

entries.definition: Calculating values at a different set of pixel locations. Methods such as nearest neighbour and averaging serve different data types.
entries.example: Nearest neighbour can move categorical water labels to a new display grid without inventing an intermediate class value.

entries.definition: Converting geographic positions from one coordinate reference system to another. Raster reprojection usually resamples the pixels onto the new grid.
entries.example: A measured UTM radar raster is reprojected for display on the browser map.

entries.definition: A raster marker for a location where a usable value is absent. It can mean the product has no coverage there or the cell was excluded.
entries.example: A transparent NoData pixel cannot be read as water, land, or an actual zero-power measurement.

entries.definition: A layer that marks whether pixels can be used or describes conditions such as an anomaly, shadow or missing data.
entries.example: The radar study combines quality information before scoring each cell. The optical comparison separately removes cloud and shadow.

entries.definition: A TIFF file that also records where its raster cells belong on Earth. It can store numeric measurements or class codes.
entries.example: A downloaded NISAR GeoTIFF can preserve calibrated power values and map coordinates for examination in QGIS.

inline.meaning: a map file that keeps each pixel’s location

entries.definition: A GeoTIFF organized so compatible software can retrieve just the blocks it needs from a server that supports byte ranges.
entries.example: The workflow can read a small area of a remote optical COG without downloading the whole satellite scene.

entries.definition: A text format for geographic features such as points, lines and polygons, with coordinates and optional properties.
entries.example: The evidence layer can use GeoJSON to store a reported outline and its source date.

entries.definition: A scientific file format that groups arrays and descriptive information in one structured container.
entries.example: One NISAR HDF5 product can store measured covariance arrays, pixel-quality masks and the acquisition details.

entries.definition: Information describing the data, such as where and when it was collected, which channels exist, its units and processing version.
entries.example: A catalogue result can list the observation's time and footprint before you open any measured pixels.

entries.definition: The record of where data came from and what was done to produce a result from it.
entries.example: A reviewed layer can record its source NISAR granule, cutout and coordinate system so somebody can trace it back to the original measurements.

entries.definition: One indexed unit of satellite data in a collection, commonly corresponding to a specific product and acquisition segment.
entries.example: The granule ID helps retrieve the exact Curuai October source even when many scenes overlap the lake.

entries.definition: A searchable list of data records, often with times, footprints, file links and browse images.
entries.example: A search can find that a GCOV product exists and list HH without providing any scientific pixel values inside the search response.

entries.definition: A viewable picture supplied to help identify or inspect a dataset before retrieving its scientific arrays.
entries.example: A thumbnail can show the general scene pattern. Use the calibrated raster for a numeric value in dB.

entries.definition: Numeric values taken from a scientific product and stored with their measurement units and spatial information.
entries.example: The NISAR HH scientific raster stores gamma0 power. Display software can transform positive power into dB for viewing or analysis.

entries.definition: Checking a user's identity before granting access to certain data or account features.
entries.example: You may see NASA catalogue listings and browse images publicly, then sign in when retrieving protected scientific files.

entries.definition: NASA's sign-in service used by Earth science data services.
entries.example: Earthdata Login can authorize requests to retrieve a NISAR science product or a Harmony result.

entries.definition: NASA's searchable index of Earth science collections, individual data granules and services.
entries.example: An ASF granule's CMR record provides its catalogue identity and links to official resources.

entries.definition: A NASA service that processes requests to transform supported Earth science data, such as returning a geographic or variable subset.
entries.example: A Harmony request can produce a small window from a selected NISAR product when the collection and service support it.

entries.definition: A selected part of a dataset, such as a limited map window, dates or a few measurement variables.
entries.example: A local NISAR crop can deliver the HH pixels over an area of interest without needing to display the whole parent scene.

entries.definition: A common specification for describing spatial datasets, when and where they apply, and how to find their files.
entries.example: An optical STAC item can list its acquisition time, scene geometry and separate reflectance and classification assets.

entries.definition: A table that shows which radar channels are available for each satellite observation.
entries.example: Find a date, then look across the HH, HV, VH and VV columns. Select a measured channel to load its image.

entries.definition: The panel that shows where the data came from, when it was collected, and what checks or limits apply.
entries.example: Near Eugene Island, open Source audit to see the older NISAR observation and the later NOAA reference separately.

entries.definition: An overlay that draws results and independent reference boundaries from a checked case. Its legend tells you what each outline represents.
entries.example: At Curuai, solid orange outlines mark exposed water where the radar screen and a separate optical image agreed.

entries.definition: A check of what a model can identify and where the data are good enough to judge its answer.
entries.example: At Atanasovsko Lake, the model withheld all predictions because the radar noise was too close to its cutoff.

entries.definition: How fully one map layer covers what is underneath it.
entries.example: Lower the radar layer’s opacity to see the coastline below it. The measured radar values stay the same.

entries.definition: A map control that moves and zooms the view so the selected radar image fits on screen.
entries.example: After panning away from Qeshm, select Fit raster to return to the recorded image.

entries.definition: The rectangle that holds the part of the radar image saved for viewing. Some pixels inside the rectangle can still be missing.
entries.example: At Eloi Bay the crop includes areas with no usable NISAR pixels. Check the grayscale image to see where the radar actually measured.

entries.definition: The area chosen for an investigation. Its boundary tells you where the work looked.
entries.example: The study area around an offshore report can include both an unusual patch and nearby ordinary water.

entries.definition: A pin that marks a location worth inspecting. Open it to see why it was marked and what evidence supports it.
entries.example: A red oil review point can mark where a separate report found a dark patch. The outline and source tell you more about its size and cause.

entries.definition: The app’s background map colors for broad features such as land and water. They help show where the radar image sits.
entries.example: Blue outside the radar image provides geographic context. Read the dated radar image and its legend to see measured values.

entries.definition: The part of the app where you choose your own study area, dates and radar channel.
entries.example: Open Manual to set the study area, then select Acquisitions to choose a particular date and HH or HV.

entries.definition: The chat controls that explain the measurements and help you select a map view using ordinary words.
entries.example: Type ‘Show me wetlands’ to open a checked example, or ‘What does dB mean?’ to read a sourced definition without changing the map.

entries.definition: A list of the times when the satellite actually observed a place. Select a date to see its available radar image.
entries.example: Qeshm has three recorded HH dates. Days between those entries have no measurement in the chart.

entries.definition: A boundary traced in a separate study or image to help check what the radar picked up.
entries.example: At Eugene Island, the dashed red outline comes from NOAA’s later observation. The solid outline shows dark NISAR pixels inside that boundary.

entries.definition: An area where the radar screen and a separate light-based image both indicate exposed water.
entries.example: The solid orange areas at Curuai show agreement on checked pixels. Water hidden by plants needs a different check.

entries.definition: A short code calculated from a file’s contents. Checking it helps tell whether the downloaded bytes match the saved file.
entries.example: Source audit lists the SHA-256 for the GeoTIFF. Matching it verifies the download’s bytes. Its scientific meaning comes from the acquisition and processing records.

entries.definition: An image made by measuring light from the surface. A satellite camera can record visible light and wavelengths beyond what our eyes can see.
entries.example: The Curuai check used a separate optical image to look for exposed water. Thick clouds can hide what is beneath them in that image.

inline.meaning: a satellite image made from light
